INTRODUCTIONM
This lesson introduces the student to the principles and operation of position detection devices, including analog and digital position-sensing circuits.
Within the field of industrial controls, inputs to circuits originate from various environments, such as light, heat, motion, pressure and humidity.
Industrial controls require accurate position detection sensors to continuously detect the position of various objects.
Let's begin the lesson on POSITION DETECTION OPERATION....................

NATURE OF POSITION
DISCUSSION
Position describes the location of an object...............
The position of an object is defined in terms of one, two, or three dimensions in respect to a reference.
Here, the position of the object is defined using one dimension.
The car's position is 3 in respect to zero.
An assembly line is a typical example of one dimensional position.
Position can be described using 2 dimensions. These dimensions are vertical and horizontal.O
The position is "(3,3)'' with respect to zero.
A typical example is an X-Y plotter which positions a stylus on a flat plane to draw various forms.
Another form of two dimensional position is related to circular motion.
Position is expressed in degrees or radians from a reference point.
A typical example is a radar scope that indicates the bearing of an object.

POSITION TRANSDUCERS
DISCUSSION
Analog position sensors are devices that change a mechanical position to an analog electrical signal.
A popular type of analog position sensor is called a resolver.
There are two types, let's start off with the induction type.
An induction resolver is a transformer with a movable primary coil and a fixed secondary coil.
The mechanical input from an object is applied to the shaft which positions the primary coil.
The electrical output is taken from the secondary coil.
As the shaft is rotated from 0 degrees to 360 degrees, the amount of flux coupling between the coils changes.
At zero degrees, the primary and secondary are displaced 90 degrees.
At 90 degrees, the primary and secondary coils are parallel and in phase.
There is maximum coupling between primary and secondary. The output goes from 0 volts to maximum.
At 180 degrees, the primary and secondary coils are again 90 degrees displaced.
There is no coupling between primary and secondary. The output returns to 0 volts.
At 270 degrees, the primary and secondary coils are again parallel. Only this time, they are not in phase.
The coupling is maximum and the output is at it's maximum negative value.
When the shaft returns to the 0 degree position, there is no coupling between primary and secondary.
For any shaft position the electrical output is different. This is a position sensor.
The voltage and position outputs produce a sine function.
However, if a linear output is required, the shaft is only allowed to rotate between 140 degrees to 220 degrees.
The voltage output is in the linear region of the curve. Eout and position output vary from positive to negative, depending on shaft position..
Which device best describes an analog inductive position sensor?
TRY AGAIN!
The analog inductive position sensor uses flux coupling between a primary coil and a secondary coil. It is not a potentiometer.
TRY AGAIN!
The analog inductive position sensor uses flux coupling between a primary coil and a secondary coil. It is not an inductor.
At which shaft angles is the output of an inductive position sensor 0?
TRY AGAIN!
At 90 and 270 degrees, the primary and secondary have maximum coupling, the output is maximum not zero.
TRY AGAIN!
The output is zero when the shaft position is 180 degrees. However, at 90 degrees, the primary and secondary have maximum coupling and the output is not 0.
The second type of resolver is a resistive device..........
Resistance resolvers are specially designed potentiometers.
The mechanical input from an object is applied to the shaft of the potentiometer which positions the wiper.
The output is taken across the wiper and one end of the resistive material.
As the position of the shaft changes, the position of the wiper changes, just like a potentiometer.
For each position, there is a specific output.
If the A and B terminals are left open, the output is resistance.
If a voltage is applied to the A and B terminals, the output is a voltage.
The device acts as a simple voltage divider.
The result is that for any position of the input shaft, the resistance or voltage output is different.
Which device best describes an analog resistance position sensor?
TRY AGAIN!
The analog resistance position sensor uses a resistive material and a wiper. It is not a transformer.
TRY AGAIN!
The analog resistance position sensor uses a resistive material and a wiper. It is not an inductor.
At which shaft position is the output of the resistance position sensor 0?
TRY AGAIN!
With the shaft positioning the wiper to the top of the resistance, the output is not 0. The entire resistance is felt at the output.
TRY AGAIN!
With the shaft positioning the wiper to about half way in the resistance, the output is not 0. About half the resistance is felt at the output.
Both position sensors use circular motion for sensing......
Even though circular positioning is the most popular, there are times when linear positioning techniques are required.
This linear position sensor operates similar to the inductive sensor. It is a linear voltage differential transformer..
It is constructed with a single primary and two balanced secondary windings connected series opposing.
With the core centered, flux coupling to each secondary is equal, the induced voltages cancel and the output is 0.
When the position of the core changes, one of the secondaries induced voltage increases and the other decreases.
This produces a positive or negative output voltage.
The output is designed to be a linear function of the core position for the extremes of core travel.
This linear position sensor operates similar to the resistance sensor. It is a linear resistance sensor.
Its operation is exactly like that of the circular resistance sensor except motion is in a straight line rather than circular.

Digital position sensors are devices that change a mechanical position to an analog electrical signal.
There are two basic types of digital position sensors......
Let's start off with the increment wheel.
An increment wheel position sensor is nothing more than a wheel placed on a prime mover or on an object.
The wheel is printed so a light or magnetic transducer may be used to sense the marks.
The increment marks represent position in reference to the zero position, indicated by the reference mark.
As the position of the wheel changes, the increment sensor produces high pulse outputs.
By counting the number of high pulse outputs, the position of the wheel can be determined.
To operate correctly, increment marks must be counted from the reference mark.
This means that the shaft must return to zero prior to each move and increment count sequence.
Each mark is a discrete point. If the position of the wheel is between marks, the position count, or the position, will not be detected.
Recall that analog position sensors have an infinite number of positions. Digital position sensors have a discrete number of positions..
In other words, the number of increment marks divide the wheel. This is called the resolution.
To determine resolution, measured in degrees per mark, you divide 360 degrees by the number of marks.
For example, the resolution of this wheel is 36 degrees per mark because there are 10 sensor marks.
Position = Resolution x Number of Marks Sensed
This means if two marks were sensed or counted, that the position of the wheel is 72 degrees from the 0 reference. Position = Resolution x Number of Marks Sensed
What is the resolution of this increment wheel?

RESOLUTION - Resolution equals the 360 degrees divided by the number of sensor marks.
If a increment wheel has 180 sensor marks, what is the position (in degrees, from 0 degrees) if 23 marks were sensed?

180 is the number of sensor marks on the increment wheel. To determine position, you must determine the resolution first.
POSITION - To determine position, you calculate resolution and then multiply the resolution times the number of sensed marks.
To overcome the disadvantage of returning the wheel to zero, an encoder wheel is used.
An encoder wheel is also placed on a prime mover or an object.
The difference is that the encoder wheel is divided into tracks with one sensor for each track.
In the plane of the sensors, a digital code is printed on the wheel for each number band.
The sensors then detect the code and output parallel digital data that represents position.
Normally, one of two different types of codes are printed on the wheel.
The 8421 code represents the binary weight of each digit from the Most Significant Bit (MSB) to the Least Significant Bit (LSB)..
The dark areas do not reflect light and produce a 0 or low output.
The light areas reflect light and produce a 1 or high output.
Note that if a magnetic pick up is used, the areas would represent magnetic and non-magnetic portions.
When the sensors are over a band, the output represents the position of the wheel by a binary number, from 0000 to 1111 in this case.
A problem with the 8421 code is that the track for each band is not the same length.
This means that as the wheel moves, the digital output does not change at the same time.
Incorrect outputs can occur during the transition between one position and another.
For example, at T1, the MSB sensor is in the band for the position 1000 but, the other sensors are in the band for 0111. The output is 1111 which is incorrect.
At T2, the two MSB sensors are in the 1000 band but, the two LSB sensors are still in the 0111 band. The output is 1011 which is still incorrect.
At T3, the output is 1001 and is still incorrect. Only the three MSB digits are in the correct band.
Finally, at T4, the output is correct. All sensors are in the correct band.
To overcome the incorrect outputs during transition, an additional track is added. The strobe track.
The strobe track is printed so that a high is produced in the center of the number band.
The high output of the strobe track is then used in external circuits to enable the output of the other sensors.
This ensures that the output of the sensors only occurs when all the sensors are in the correct number band, thus eliminating transition errors.
Another method of eliminating transition errors is to use a different type of code on the wheel, the Grey Code.
Look carefully at the binary numbers that represent each position.
Notice that only one digit changes from a 1 to 0 or changes from a 0 to 1 for each change in position.
The one digit change occurs both in the clockwise and counterclockwise direction.
By using the Grey Code, the output errors in transition are eliminated.
You have probably noticed that both the 8421 and Grey Code wheels used 4 bits.
This does not have to be the case. Any number of tracks can be used.
However, the number tracks determine the resolution of the wheel. The more tracks, the more the wheel is divided.
The resolution of a code wheel equals 360 degrees divided by two to the N power, N is the number of tracks.
Recall in digital electronics that the number of digit combinations depends on the number of positions or 2 to the N power.
For example, the resolution of a wheel with four tracks (not including the strobe track) is 22.5 degrees per number band.
If another track is added, five tracks, the resolution is 11.25 degrees per number band.

POSITION DETECTION OPERATION
EXPERIMENT
Physical position sensing provides an electrical readout (analog or digital) or provides feedback to a controller, which automatically positions an object.

This basic block diagram applies to any type of position sensing circuit regardless of prime mover, analog or digital circuitry, or angular or linear motion. The operator sets position controls, and the prime mover executes the command...

As the object moves, the position-sensing circuit input feedback to circuits that send signals to a summing circuit. The summing point circuit compares the input position (vi) to the actual position signal (vF)...

If the comparison voltage is different, an error signal (ve) drives the amplifier, which in turn drives the prime mover. When actual position (vF) equals position desired (vi), the prime mover error driver signal (ve) equals zero and the prime mover stops...

The actual circuits within the block diagram are basic analog or digital circuits applied to the mechanics of positioning. This schematic shows the basic circuitry used in the experiment to test a simple closed loop position sensing system...

The circuit uses a pick-off voltage developed by a rotating potentiometer connected to the motor as the position sensor voltage (vF). This position signal is then compared to the MOTOR SPEED control (reference input) voltage (vi)...

The two voltages are compared in summing point circuit. U1A and U1B sum the two inputs. Notice that inputs to U1A and U1B are configured in opposite positions. The reference input voltage (vi) to U1A is connected to the + input (Pin 3); (vi) to U1B is connected to the - input (Pin 6)...
The position input voltage (vF) to U1A is connected to the - input (Pin 2); and (vF) to U1B is connected to the + input (Pin 5).

Summing point circuit outputs are sent to U2C through the Proportional Section of the PID and then to the pulse width modulator (PWM). The PWM sends the pulse-modulated signal to the amplifier (U3) to drive the motor...

The output of U1A is inverted by U2A. U2A output is sent to the amplifier (U3) and to U2B. The signal is sent to the amplifier (U3 Pin 7) as a clockwise input signal. The signal sent to U2B is inverted and sent to the amplifier as a counterclockwise input signal...
Notice that the amplifier not only amplifies the motor drive signal, but it also controls the clockwise and counterclockwise rotational voltages.

The amplifier output signal drives the motor if there is any difference between the reference input voltage (vi) and the position sensor voltage (vF). Zero difference voltages from the PWM allow the motor to remain in a fixed position...
